title: Top Comments: Dark Matter Apparent by Its Absence
excerpt: If you’ve read many of my diaries, you know that I’m interested in the topic of dark matter and follow its developments. Dark matter was invoked to explain what holds galaxies together…
content:
Here at Top Comments we strive to nourish community by rounding up some of the site’s best, funniest, most informative commentary, and we depend on your help!! Here’s how to submit nominations in DK6: If you see a comment by another Kossack that deserves wider recognition, please send it either to topcomments at gmail dot com or via kosmail to topcomments- either search for user @topcomments, or click that link then click “send message”!) by 9:30pm Eastern for inclusion in that day’s diary. Please, please include a few words about why you sent it in as well as your user name (even if you think we know it already :-)), so we can credit you with the find! It’s especially helpful if you include a link to the comment you’re nominating… hover over the comment and you’ll see Share and Report options. Click Share, then choose ”copy url” and paste that into your message to us.

If you’ve read many of my diaries, you know that I’m interested in the topic of dark matter and follow its developments. Dark matter was invoked to explain what holds galaxies together, since the speed of rotation of the stars in the arms of spiral galaxies was too fast for the mass of the visible matter present to hold on to by gravity. Since then, an argument has developed between those who favor dark matter as an explanation for this phenomenon, and others favor the hypothesis that the force of gravity deviates from Newton’s Law at astronomical separations (MOND). In 2018, a discovery was made that bolstered the dark matter side of the argument: a galaxy that appeared to have much less dark matter as a proportion of its mass than any other known galaxy at the time. I mentioned this discovery in one of my diaries. The galaxy itself was diffuse of stars, and the amount of dark matter was deduced by measuring the rotation speed of the stars in orbit around the galaxy. The existence of such a galaxy implies that there’s nothing wrong with Newton’s law at astronomical distances (which were clearly obeyed in this instance), and so dark matter really is necessary to hold galaxies together.

Astronomers have since discovered two more such galaxies, both in the neighborhood of the first one, and further, they have developed a hypothesis for how these three galaxies formed their current structures, which involved their loss of dark matter. These discoveries clearly demonstrate the important role dark matter plays in more usual galaxies that contain dark matter.

The title image of this diary shows the three galaxies with reduced dark matter content. They are labelled DF2, DF9 and DF4, and you can barely see them in that image. More detailed images of the three galaxies are shown below:

They look kind of sickly, compared to more typical galaxies, and this highlights one of the roles of dark matter in the lives of galaxies: the gravity due to dark matter helps to condense gas clouds more quickly, thus catalyzing the process of star formation.

“What this is showing is that dark matter is … not just a modification of gravity,” said Keim, who is an author of the new study. If you segregate ordinary matter from dark matter, you’d expect that the dark matter–lacking galaxies would struggle to form stars — and that’s what DF2, DF4, and DF9 show.

The fact that all three of these highly unusual galaxies lie along a line in the same neighborhood suggests that there’s more to the story, and there is. Astronomers have come up with a hypothesis for their origin. Because dark matter interacts with other matter only through the force of gravity, when a collision between two ordinary galaxies, which are mixtures of ordinary and dark matter, the ordinary matter is stopped by running into other ordinary matter while the dark matter speed through the encounter without hesitation. This is reminiscent of the famous Bullet Cluster photograph, where two large clusters of galaxies collide, and, ordinary matter is emitting x-rays, shown in pink, at the center of the collision, while the dark matter, detected by gravitational lensing, shown in blue, is clearly traveling unimpeded beyond the collision. It is conceivable that a collision between two galaxies traveling at high enough relative speeds could strip each other of dark matter in this way.

However, there are other possible scenarios.

Kinwah Wu(opens a new tab), a theoretical astrophysicist at University College London, noted that the triplet does not exhibit any of the fluid, wispy features(opens a new tab) that one would expect to see after a galactic collision. He suggests that, in this case, DF2, DF4, and DF9 were passing through a large group of massive galaxies. This outsize rabble then stripped the triplet of all their dark matter during their ill-fated voyage.

It’s a bit ironic that finding galaxies that contain little to no dark matter turn out to bolster the existence of dark matter. These dark matter deficient galaxies appear as diffuse and faint, with a diminished capability of forming new stars. They don’t look like “normal” galaxies, which suggests that the normal galactic process of star formation requires the presence of dark matter. MOND is incapable of providing an explanation for any of this. So I guess we’re stuck with dark matter.
